Average neonatal body mass in the water opossum is remarkably low, with newborns weighing a mere quarter of a gram at birth (0.25 grams) [Wwb = 0.25 grams]. This minuscule size, typical of many marsupials, is accompanied by an extremely brief gestation period of only 13 days [tg = 13 days] when measured at a stable core temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. Following this rapid internal development, the altricial newborn must immediately crawl to the mother's pouch to commence an extended period of lactation. The onset of suckling represents a critical transition, as the neonate is entirely dependent on teat attachment for its nutritional needs. The duration of this lactation period is relatively prolonged, reflecting the species' need for substantial morphological development outside the womb. Weaning from maternal milk occurs after approximately 60 days [tx = approximately 60 days] at 35 °C [T = 35 °C], at which point the offspring have achieved a wet weight of around 75 grams [Wwx = around 75 grams] and begin the transition to a diet of aquatic invertebrates.

Considerable growth is required before the young attain sexual maturity, a milestone that is not reached until well after weaning. Available data indicate that puberty in captive individuals is reached at 304 days after birth [tp = 304 days after birth] under thermoneutral conditions of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. At this developmental stage, the body mass of the sub-adult is approximately 400 grams [Wwp = approximately 400 grams]. The onset of reproductive activation marks a definitive shift in physiological priorities, as the now-mature individual must balance its own continued somatic growth against the energetic demands of territory establishment and mate acquisition. This relatively long pre-reproductive period—spanning nearly a full year—is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes the attainment of a robust adult body size before investing in offspring. Body condition during the juvenile stage is likely a strong predictor of future reproductive success in this semiaquatic predator.

Reproductive output in the water opossum is modest but consistent with its marsupial life-history strategy. Females typically produce a litter of four pups per reproductive event [N_R_i = four pups per reproductive event], and field records suggest they can produce between two and three litters each year [F_R_i = between two and three litters each year]. This reproductive schedule, combining a moderate litter size with a relatively high annual frequency, results in a considerable lifetime reproductive potential. At the ambient temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], which approximates the species' thermoneutral zone, the metabolic costs of gestation and lactation are likely minimized, allowing for efficient energy conversion into offspring biomass. The relatively short gestation period is partially offset by the extended pouch life and subsequent lactation, during which the altricial young undergo most of their critical organ development. This pattern of investing heavily in a small number of well-developed offspring per event is a common theme among small-bodied didelphid marsupials.

Adult body size in Chironectes minimus shows considerable variation, though the maximum recorded wet weight for a fully grown individual is approximately 923 grams [Wwi = approximately 923 grams], a figure that exceeds the typical range of 604 to 790 grams frequently cited in field guides. This ultimate body mass is attained only after the completion of all major growth phases. The basal metabolic rate of a non-reproducing adult at rest has been measured at 366.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 366.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] under thermoneutral conditions at 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This metabolic rate reflects the substantial energetic cost of maintaining a high-quality pelage and a relatively large brain for a mammal of this size. The species' semiaquatic habits impose additional thermoregulatory demands; however, the dense, water-repellent fur provides effective insulation in the cool streams and rivers it inhabits across Central and South America.

Longevity data for the water opossum are limited, but a captive specimen was documented to have survived for three point one years [am = three point one years]. This relatively short lifespan, which corresponds to approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] when extrapolated under ideal captive conditions at 35 °C [T = 35 °C], is characteristic of small-bodied dasyuromorphian and didelphimorphian marsupials, which tend to exhibit rapid life histories. The combination of a modest adult mass, a high reproductive rate, and a short maximum lifespan suggests a strategy of fast population turnover, typical of an r-selected species occupying a predator-rich but productive aquatic niche. The maximum lifespan in the wild is almost certainly lower than these captive records indicate, constrained by predation from larger carnivores and the risks associated with foraging in aquatic environments. Overall, the life history of Chironectes minimus reflects a tightly integrated suite of traits adapted to its unique ecological role as the world's only fully aquatic marsupial.
